steps.body: Multiplying by 2 makes a **double**: two equal copies of the same amount. The model pairs 5 with another 5, so 5 × 2 = 5 + 5 = 10. Doubling is repeated addition with exactly two equal addends.
steps.narration: Multiplying by 2 makes a **double**: two equal copies of the same amount. The model pairs 5 with another 5, so 5 × 2 = 5 + 5 = 10. Doubling is repeated addition with exactly two equal addends.

steps.body: Pair the total to test whether two equal groups are possible.

widget.prompt: 7 + 8 makes 15. Pair all 15 counters to test whether 15 can be split into two equal groups.
widget.evenFeedback: One counter is still unpaired. A double has two equal groups, so its total must pair with no leftover.
widget.unfinishedFeedback: Finish pairing the counters before deciding whether two equal groups are possible.
widget.successFeedback: One of the 15 counters is left over. So 7 + 8 is not a double; it is one more than 7 + 7.

options.label: No — a double uses the same addend twice
Yes — consecutive addends make a double

predict.reveal: A double uses the same addend twice, such as 7 + 7. The sum 7 + 8 is one more than that double.

steps.body: Translate ×2 into the addition it hides.
explanationVariants: 7 × 2 is two groups of 7 — the number plus itself: 7 + 7 = 14.
Picture both hands holding 7 marbles each: one 7, another 7.

options.feedback: 7 + 2 = 9 joins the factor instead of doubling. The 2 says how many 7s to take: two of them.
7 × 7 doubles the wrong thing — it makes seven GROUPS of 7 (49). A double takes the number twice.
72 glues the digits together. The × asks you to take 7 two times, not to write 7 and 2 side by side.

steps.body: Big number to double? **Split it, double the parts, rejoin.** Double 8: split into 5 and 3, double each — 10 and 6 — then 10 + 6 = 16. Splitting into a friendly 5 or 10 makes any double quick.
Straight recall — no scaffolding this time.
explanationVariants: Split-double-rejoin: double 5 is 10, double 3 is 6, and 10 + 6 = 16.

commonErrors.feedback: 10 adds 8 + 2. The 2 isn't joining the pile — it says take the 8 twice: 8 + 8.
64 is 8 × 8 — the 8 got doubled as a FACTOR. A double takes the number itself twice.
82 writes the digits side by side. Multiply means 8, twice: 8 + 8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Say the double out loud: 8 plus 8.

steps.body: Doubling **again and again** makes a chain.

widget.prompt: Each number doubles the one before it. Put the doubling chain in order, smallest first.

misorderFeedback.feedback: 16 landed before 8 — but 16 is 8's double, so it comes after. Each link is twice the one before.

widget.missFeedback: Start at 2 and double your way up: 2, then 4, then 8, then 16.
widget.successFeedback: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 — each link is the last one, doubled. Chains like this power the ×4 and ×8 tricks soon.

steps.body: Spot the double hiding in a story.
explanationVariants: The same 9 pages happen twice a day — a double: 9 × 2 = 18.
Morning 9 plus evening 9: identical parts, so 9 + 9 = 18.

widget.prompt: Rico reads 9 pages every morning and 9 pages every evening. How many pages does he read each day?

options.feedback: The same 9, twice a day — a double. 18 pages.
The 2 counts the reading TIMES, not extra pages. Two sessions of 9 means 9 taken twice.
9 × 9 would be nine sessions of 9 pages. Rico reads twice a day — double the 9, don't square it.
That doubles the number of sessions and loses the pages. The pages — 9 of them — are what happens twice.

steps.body: A double, then a double again.
hints: First find the whole first load — cars on BOTH decks.
7 cars × 2 decks = 14 cars on the first trip.
The return trip carries double that: 14 + 14.
explanationVariants: First trip: 7 × 2 = 14 cars. Return: double 14 = 28 cars.
Double twice: 7 doubles to 14 (two decks), and 14 doubles to 28 (the return load).

widget.prompt: A ferry carries 7 cars on each of its 2 decks. The return trip carries double the whole first load. How many cars ride the return trip?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 is the FIRST trip's load — step one done! The return trip doubles that whole load.
16 adds 2 to 14 instead of doubling. Doubling 14 means 14 + 14.
21 adds one more 7 to 14. But the return doubles the WHOLE load of 14 — add another full 14.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two doubles: 7 across 2 decks first, then that whole answer taken twice.

takeaways: ×2 = the number plus itself — an addition you already know.
Double big numbers by splitting, doubling the parts, and rejoining.
Doubles chain: doubling again and again builds new facts fast.
steps.teaser: fives ride the clock and tens ride the zero — the two friendliest fact families.

concept.body: Quick rewind. ×2 asks for a number **twice**. Hold up the fact on your hands: 4 × 2 is one hand of 4 and another hand of 4 — count them all: 8. If you can add a number to itself, you already own every ×2 fact.

explanationVariants: Two groups of 4: count 4, then 4 more — 8.

options.feedback: 6 adds 4 + 2. The 2 says take the 4 twice: 4 + 4.
16 is 4 × 4 — that doubles too far. One doubling of 4 lands on 8.
